hints: Measure line X-Y on your printed Fig. 1.1 in millimetres with a ruler and note the magnification printed under the micrograph.
Remember the magnification triangle where image size = actual size x magnification, so rearrange to find actual size.
Convert your answer from mm to micrometres using $1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$ and round to one decimal place.
walkthrough:
Measure the Image and State the Formula**
You are looking at a real size that has been enlarged 16000 times. Measure X-Y carefully in mm. On the paper this is about $40 \text{ mm}$. The governing relationship is $\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image length}}{\text{actual length}}$, so rearranged: $\text{actual length} = \frac{\text{image length}}{\text{magnification}}$.

Substitute and Convert Units**
Put the numbers in: $\text{actual width} = 40 \text{ mm} / 16000 = 0.0025 \text{ mm}$. A millimetre is far too big for a cell organelle, so convert to micrometres: $0.0025 \times 1000 = 2.5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$. That is to one decimal place as $2.5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$.
Final answer: actual length = image length / magnification; image X-Y = 40 mm, $40 \text{ mm} / 16000 = 0.0025 \text{ mm} = 2.5 \text{ } \mu\text{m}$

hints: Look closely at organelle A - it has an outer boundary and a much folded inner membrane forming shelf-like cristae inside.
Think about which organelle needs a large inner membrane surface to make ATP by aerobic respiration.
walkthrough:
Recognise the Mitochondrion**
The sausage-shaped body with a double membrane is the giveaway. The inner membrane is folded inward to form cristae, which you can see as wavy lines across organelle A. That folding is unique to mitochondria in animal cells.

Link Structure to Role**
Those cristae hold the electron transport chain and ATP synthase. So this is the site where aerobic respiration happens, using oxygen to release energy from glucose and make ATP, the energy currency used to drive active transport, muscle contraction, protein synthesis and other work.
Final answer: name: mitochondrion; role: site of aerobic respiration to produce / supply ATP for cell activities.

hints: Look at structure B below the mitochondrion - focus on the long parallel stacks of membranes studded with tiny dark dots.
Think about what those tiny dots are and how they distinguish rough from smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
walkthrough:
Recognise Stacked Membranes With Dots**
Structure B is a set of flattened, parallel membrane sacs called cisternae running across the bottom of the picture. The surfaces look rough and grainy because they are covered in tiny black dots.

Use Ribosomes as the Clue**
Those dots are ribosomes attached to the cytosolic face of the membranes. Endoplasmic reticulum with attached ribosomes is by definition rough ER, specialised to fold, modify and transport proteins made by those ribosomes.
Final answer: name: rough endoplasmic reticulum; reason: membranes have ribosomes attached / studded on surface for protein synthesis.
